title: The Soul Is Always Praying
hookLine: Rav Kook wrote of the soul's longing for the infinite
tomorrow: what changes when you say "you" instead of "it"?

lines: ONE A.M., ONE TAB STILL OPEN.
I DON'T EVEN KNOW WHAT I WANT.
cards: One in the morning. A browser tab that never gets closed: a summer theater program in New York, photos of a black stage, a deadline in red. Noa has read the page so many times she could perform it.
She types to a friend, then deletes it, then types it again: i don't even know what i want from it. Some wants come with a name and a price.

Others just ache, and the thing on the screen is only where the ache landed tonight. A rabbi in Jerusalem, Abraham Isaac Kook, wrote a great deal about that second kind. He didn't treat it as a problem.

teach.b: Rav Kook taught that the soul is always praying. Not only in synagogue, not only when words come out: underneath everything, it keeps reaching toward its source, the infinite, the way a flame keeps leaning up.
In his telling, the prayers in the prayer book are the moments that hidden prayer finally becomes audible. That's the fact to repeat tonight: for Kook, prayer doesn't start the longing.
It lets you hear the longing that was already going. He was reading an old picture.
Proverbs says, "The spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD." And a psalm says it outright: "My soul yearneth, yea, even pineth for the courts of the LORD." So what does that do with a one a.m. ache?
Kook doesn't tell anyone to crush it, and he doesn't say every want is holy either. He suggests listening underneath.
A wish for a stage, a city, a person can be a small window onto a larger reach, the soul's pull toward something without an edge.
The program may be right or wrong for Noa. The longing itself isn't a mistake. It might be a prayer, and an honest one.

how: Rav Kook's writings on the soul's longing and on prayer are studied in many yeshivot and adult classes, and his idea that the soul is always praying is often taught alongside the prayer book.

o: a craving to fix every flaw in yourself
a homesick feeling for the place you grew up
a constant inner reach toward God, the infinite source

games.q: Rav Kook on longing — tap the pairs.
p: where the hidden prayer becomes audible
the spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD
a window onto a larger reach

s: for Rav Kook, longing is a weakness to be trained out
he treats it as the soul's own motion toward its source.
Kook taught that the soul prays even when no words are said
in his telling, spoken prayer lets that constant prayer be heard.
Kook taught that every want is holy just as it is
he asks you to listen underneath a want, not to bless it as it stands.

games.q: your brother keeps refreshing a sneaker drop at midnight and says he feels empty when he gets them anyway. what would Rav Kook's idea notice first?
o: the want might be a small window onto a bigger longing.
wanting things is the problem; he should stop wanting.
the shoes will satisfy him if he gets the right pair.
games.why: Kook doesn't crush longing or bless every want. he listens under it for the soul's reach toward something without an edge.

practice: Close your eyes and let one longing come up, the one that keeps showing up late at night. Don't solve it and don't argue with it. Sit beside it, and ask it gently what it's reaching for underneath.

wordCard.voice: The soul longs: Rav Kook's teaching that the soul reaches, without pause, toward its source, and that prayer is that reach said out loud.

orig.note: Hebrew: soul, breath. the word Kook uses for the soul that is always praying.

carryVoice: Pocket this: the soul is always praying. In Kook's telling, the ache is already a kind of prayer.
